title: WaterAccu vs smart switch: a comparison
excerpt: WaterAccu vs smart switch? Controlling your electric boiler smartly is a good idea. In this blog, we compare the two options!
contentHtml:
Do you have solar panels? An affordable way to make better use of your solar energy is with an electric boiler with smart controls. Are you wondering what the additional benefits of the Nymo are? In this blog, we explain the differences between the two systems and present the results of an analysis we conducted to see exactly how much difference there is in savings between the two systems.

Why choose an electric boiler with smart controls?

Solar panels are a brilliant way to drive the energy transition and ensure that households can use more clean energy. The Netherlands ranks first in the EU in terms of solar panels per capita, and almost 1/3 of households have solar panels on their roofs!

However, the problem is that there is a mismatch between household energy consumption and solar energy production. In general, households consume the most energy in the morning and evening, while sunshine peaks between noon and 3 p.m. As a result, only 30-40% of the energy generated is used within the household, and the rest is fed back into the grid. What a waste!

This was not yet a major problem for households, thanks to the net metering scheme. However, this scheme will be abolished at the end of 2026, making solar panels much less profitable. In addition, energy companies introduced monthly feed-in charges for feeding solar energy back into the grid.

What is the solution? Utilize more of your own generation! If you utilize more solar energy (called “self-consumption”), you pay less feed-in tariffs and need less electricity from the grid. One way to do this is to run an electric boiler on surplus solar energy and use the hot tap water later when needed. Here we compare two solutions to achieve this: a “smart switch” and the WaterAccu from Solyx Energy.

What is a smart switch? And how does it work?

A smart switch is an addition to your power outlet, which you can then use to connect other devices. Examples include the Energy Socket from Homewizard and the EcoSwitch Pi from Ecosoft. These smart switches are designed to monitor your device’s energy consumption. But they also offer additional features, including the ability to switch on devices when surplus solar energy is available, hence the name “smart switch.” This feature can be used to control an electric boiler, switching on the heating element once a certain threshold for surplus solar energy has been reached.

What is the WaterAccu? And how does this compare to the smart switch?

The WaterAccu works differently than a smart switch. The main difference is that a switch simply turns on or off. This means that the boiler is either running at full power or off. The WaterAccu varies the power to the boiler. So it’s not just on or off, but exactly the amount of solar energy that is left over is sent to the boiler. The disadvantage: the WaterAccu has a higher purchase price than a smart switch.

Due to variations in cloud cover and consumption throughout the day, the amount of energy generated varies at any given moment. Ideally, you want your boiler to be heated solely by solar energy, and this is exactly what the WaterAccu does. When the amount of solar energy generated decreases, the WaterAccu will adjust the power supply. The graphs below show an example of this over a 24-hour period.

Explanation of the upper graph:

  • The orange line shows the total generation of solar energy.
  • The blue line shows household consumption.
  • The green area shows the unused solar energy, which is precisely the amount that the WaterAccu will utilize.
  • The Nymo sends exactly the amount of unused power to the electric boiler.

Explanation of the bottom graph:

  • Grid input, or the use of electricity from the grid, occurs when no solar energy is being generated but household appliances are switched on.
  • All solar energy is utilized, and there is no feed-in of electricity to the grid!

A smart switch uses less solar energy and increases electricity consumption from the grid.

Above, it is clear to see that at around 10:45, the switch-on threshold of the smart switch is reached and the electric boiler is switched on.

These differences naturally lead to a difference in savings. To find out exactly how much, the two scenarios were modeled over an entire year.

Explanation of the upper graph:

  • The orange line shows the total generation of solar energy.
  • The blue line shows household consumption.
  • The purple line shows that around 10:45, the switch-on threshold of the smart switch is reached, and the electric boiler is switched on (at full power).
  • The green area shows the amount of unused solar energy that the smart switch will utilize.
  • The yellow area shows the solar energy that is still being fed back into the grid.

A considerable amount of surplus solar energy is consumed on this day. However, due to its simple on/off function, it is not as accurate as the WaterAccu; if there is a dip in the availability of solar energy, additional mains power is even used to supply the boiler with power.

Explanation of the bottom graph:

  • Grid input, or the use of electricity from the grid, occurs when no solar energy is being generated but household appliances are switched on.
  • In addition, solar power is still fed back into the electricity grid when the available surplus solar energy is not used.
  • In addition, during periods of low solar energy generation, additional grid power is used.

Conclusion: The WaterAccu saves almost twice as much as a smart switch.

The study is based on the assumption that the household initially heats tap water using a central heating combi boiler.

    • The savings with a WaterAccu are around 362 euros per year.
    • The savings with a smart switch are around 151 euros per year.

The conclusions:

  • Both solutions deliver savings, and are therefore a good step forward!
  • The savings achieved with the WaterAccu are more than twice as high as those achieved with the smart switch.
  • The most ideal threshold value was used for this study, based on the annual data. It is unlikely that a household would be able to choose this value as favorably—unless it is actively changed during the year based on the predicted weather conditions. This is despite the fact that this switch-on threshold is also the parameter with the greatest effect on savings.
  • Despite the higher investment costs of the WaterAccu compared to a smart switch, households will save significantly more money after 3 years with the WaterAccu. In addition, the WaterAccu has extra smart features such as automatic legionella protection, so there is no hassle or interference required after installation.
  • Feed-in costs, which will increase the savings made by the WaterAccu, have not been taken into account.
  • Heating with an electric boiler without smart features is relatively expensive. So if you already have a boiler, purchasing the WaterAccu is a no-brainer, because it will pay for itself in just over a year!

Discussion of the model

Here we discuss in more detail how the analysis was performed and what assumptions were made.

A typical household with four members was used as the basis for this analysis. The household has a 200-liter boiler and 16 solar panels with a capacity of 6.4 kWp. Three “standard” days were generated using realistic solar radiation and data on the household’s energy consumption. A summer day (sunny), a winter day (little sun), and an autumn/spring day (cloudy). These were extrapolated over a year.

Model assumptions:

  • No net metering scheme – this will end in 2027.
  • No feed-in costs – this will also be reviewed in a few years, so it has been left out of consideration.
  • The smart switch is switched on continuously throughout the year (set to 1.2 kW) – this value has been chosen to be favorable for the smart switch. It is important to note that households that choose a cut-in cannot determine the ideal value as accurately.
  • Once the smart switch turns on the boiler, it remains on until the boiler is fully heated.
  • The household uses an average amount of hot water, which requires the boiler to be reheated every day.

For reference, a simple “dumb” electric boiler was also modeled, which automatically switches on when hot water is used. It was assumed that this was in the morning and evening. The results were also compared with a traditional setup in which tap water is heated with a central heating combi boiler, which works according to the same logic as the simple electric boiler.
